subject: Physics
description: Nucleus, isotopes, half-life, fission vs fusion, mass defect E=mc², chain reaction, reactors

questions.stem: The nucleus of an atom contains:

options.option_text: Protons (positive charge) and neutrons (neutral) — collectively called nucleons

questions.explanation: Atomic structure: NUCLEUS (protons + neutrons; ~10⁻¹⁵ m, 99.9% of atomic mass); ELECTRONS orbit nucleus (~10⁻¹⁰ m). Atomic number Z = number of protons. Mass number A = protons + neutrons. ISOTOPES — same Z, different A (e.g., ¹H, ²H/D, ³H/T; ²³⁵U, ²³⁸U). Strong nuclear force binds nucleons (~100x electromagnetic; very short range, ~1 fm). Discoveries — Rutherford 1911 (nucleus, α-scattering); Chadwick 1932 (neutron); Anderson 1932 (positron, antimatter); Pauli 1930 / Reines-Cowan 1956 (neutrino).

questions.stem: The half-life of a radioactive substance is:

options.option_text: The total lifetime of the substance
The time taken for HALF of the original radioactive nuclei to decay (a constant for each isotope)
The time it takes to be detected
Half the time of one full radioactive cycle

questions.explanation: Half-life (T½) — time for half the original nuclei to decay. Constant for a given isotope (independent of physical/chemical conditions). After n half-lives, the surviving fraction = (1/2)ⁿ. Examples: ³H tritium 12.3 yr; ¹⁴C 5,730 yr (used in carbon-dating); ¹³¹I 8 days (used in thyroid imaging + therapy); ²³⁵U 704 million years; ²³⁸U 4.5 billion years; ⁴⁰K 1.3 billion years (used to date rocks); ¹³⁷Cs 30 years (post-Chernobyl/Fukushima fallout). Decay constant λ = ln 2 / T½. Activity A = λN; measured in becquerel (Bq, 1 decay/s) or curie (Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq).

questions.stem: In nuclear FISSION (used in nuclear reactors and atom bombs):

options.option_text: Two light nuclei fuse to form a heavier nucleus
A heavy nucleus (e.g., U-235) splits into two lighter nuclei + neutrons + energy
An electron is emitted from the nucleus

questions.explanation: FISSION — heavy nucleus splits. Discovered 1938 by Otto Hahn + Lise Meitner + Fritz Strassmann. Example: ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + ~200 MeV energy. Released neutrons can trigger further fissions → CHAIN REACTION. Critical mass — minimum mass for sustained chain reaction (uranium-235 ~52 kg sphere; can be smaller with reflector). Atom bomb (uncontrolled chain reaction); nuclear reactor (controlled, with moderator + control rods). Hiroshima 'Little Boy' (Aug 6, 1945) — U-235 gun-type. Nagasaki 'Fat Man' (Aug 9, 1945) — Pu-239 implosion-type. FUSION (opposite) — light nuclei combine; powers stars, hydrogen bomb, tokamak research (ITER). E = mc² governs both.

questions.stem: Einstein's famous equation E = mc² describes:

options.option_text: Mass-energy equivalence — even tiny mass converts to enormous energy (since c² is huge)

questions.explanation: E = mc² (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s). 1 g of matter converted entirely to energy = (10⁻³)(3×10⁸)² = 9 × 10¹³ J ≈ 21,500 tons of TNT (= about Hiroshima yield). In nuclear reactions, only a small fraction (~0.1%) of mass converts. MASS DEFECT — the mass of a nucleus is slightly less than the sum of its individual nucleons; the missing mass appears as binding energy. Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon — fusion + fission both move toward Fe-56 → release energy. Stars: hydrogen → helium fusion (proton-proton chain in sun, CNO cycle in heavier stars); supernovae produce elements heavier than iron via r-process.

questions.stem: The MOST common moderator used in Indian PHWR (Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor) nuclear reactors is:
questions.explanation: MODERATOR — slows down neutrons (fast neutrons → thermal neutrons, more likely to cause fission of U-235). Common moderators: HEAVY WATER (D₂O — used in PHWRs / CANDU; expensive but allows use of natural uranium without enrichment). LIGHT WATER (H₂O — used in PWR/BWR; cheaper but absorbs more neutrons → requires enriched U-235); GRAPHITE (used in earlier UK Magnox + Soviet RBMK; Chernobyl was graphite-moderated). India's nuclear programme — 3-stage: Stage 1 PHWR with natural U; Stage 2 fast breeder with Pu + thorium; Stage 3 thorium-based reactors. Tarapur was the first nuclear power plant (1969, BWR design from US). India has 23 operational reactors (~7,500 MWe, ~3% of grid). Kudankulam (TN) — VVER design with Russia.

questions.stem: When a radioactive nucleus emits an ALPHA particle, the resulting nucleus has:

options.option_text: Same atomic number, same mass number
Atomic number reduced by 2; mass number reduced by 4
Atomic number increased by 1; mass number unchanged
Atomic number reduced by 1; mass number unchanged

questions.explanation: Alpha (α) particle = helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons; ⁴₂He). Alpha decay: ᴬ₂X → ᴬ⁻⁴₂₋₂Y + ⁴₂He. Example: ²³⁸U → ²³⁴Th + α. BETA-MINUS (β⁻) decay: a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton + electron + antineutrino → atomic number INCREASES by 1; mass number unchanged. Example: ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + e⁻ + ν̄. BETA-PLUS (β⁺): proton → neutron + positron + neutrino → atomic number decreases by 1. GAMMA (γ) decay: high-energy photon emitted; no change in atomic or mass number — nucleus drops from excited to ground state. Penetrating power: α (stopped by paper) < β (stopped by aluminium foil) < γ (needs lead/concrete).

questions.stem: If 8 g of a radioactive substance has a half-life of 4 days, how much will remain after 16 days?
questions.explanation: 16 days = 4 half-lives (16 / 4 = 4). After n half-lives, the remaining fraction = (1/2)ⁿ = (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. Remaining = 8 × 1/16 = 0.5 g. Step-wise: Day 0 → 8 g; Day 4 → 4 g; Day 8 → 2 g; Day 12 → 1 g; Day 16 → 0.5 g. Note — the decay is exponential, not linear; after 4 half-lives, ~93.75% has decayed.
